stories.title: The Locksmith's Refusal
stories.text:
Gorven the Conjurer had spent forty years opening locks that should never yield. Now, in the ash-choked aftermath of the Remaking, the Dominion auditors wanted him to forge something impossible: a lock that could hold a consciousness-fragment prisoner so utterly that it would forget it had ever been whole. "No," he said, setting down his bone-picks on the scarred workbench of his hideaway in Keshtir's Lampwick Quarter. The Lead Auditor's shadow fell across the doorway. "You will, or your daughter starves with the rest of Crimport's refugees."

Gorven had heard this song before. Three times they'd threatened her. Three times he'd caved, forged their locks, enabled their hoarding of consciousness-dust and phantom-wealth. But something had broken in him last month when he watched a child—no older than his daughter had been—weeping over a vial of her own stolen memory, unable to reassemble herself. He stood. At sixty, his hands still remembered every pin and tumbler, every harmonic frequency that made metal sing. "I'm going to teach her to pick locks instead," he said quietly.

stories.title: The Reef-Guard's First Tide
stories.text:
Kess of the Sunken Reaches had been a thief for seventeen winters. Now, standing on the pearl-platform of the Sapphire Deep two fathoms below the surface, she held the title of Reef-Guard—a role she'd stolen from a drowning captain and a oath she'd sworn in blood-salt to the dying god whose temple had once housed the Keeper of Pearls. The harmonics shifted a quarter-note flat. The Tear of the Drowned God—the cosmic seal holding back the abyss—trembled. Kess felt it in her bones, in the pressure of the water against her consciousness-marked skin. Something vast was pressing from beneath. "The Deepkin must renew the covenant," the eldest reef-singer said, her voice a subsonic hum that rippled through Kess's teeth. "Five willing souls, offered before the dark-moon. Or the Tear breaks, and the abyss floods all lands."

Kess had been a thief. She knew the language of impossible choices.

stories.title: The Glass-Painter's Commission
stories.text:
The Dominion's commission was elegant in its cruelty: forge a lens that could read phantom-documents. If the auditors could see through the lies, they could collapse the Counter-Archive's resistance in a season. Sella, the glass-forger of Keshtir's Lampwick Quarter, accepted the work. Then she did something they never expected—she made it. The focusing-glass emerged from the kiln perfect: starlight-sharp, mind-clear, capable of reading through seven layers of deception simultaneously. The auditors wept when they tested it. With this, they could reconstruct the true ledgers, track every sabotage, identify every bone-singer hiding in plain sight. Sella delivered it herself, walking into the administrative heart of Keshtir with the lens cradled in her palms like a newborn child. "Beautiful work," the Chief Auditor said, lifting it to the light. "You've earned your family's ration-tier elevated to—"

"There's a flaw," Sella interrupted. "A small one. Only reveals itself in sunlight at a certain angle. I wanted to warn you before you relied on it in the field."

The Auditor smiled. Reliability meant everything to the Dominion.

stories.title: The Wyvern's Mercy
stories.text:
Vrekka the Fragment-Hoarder had accumulated consciousness-dust for three centuries, a mountain of severed souls compressed into crystal vials stacked in her Ironspine caverns. The Remaking should have destroyed her. Instead, it transformed her hunger into something she'd never imagined: a question. Why did she hoard? She summoned the refugee child—the one the Dominion had tried to execute by consciousness-extraction, the one Vrekka's own talons had plucked from a furnace-house in Keshtir. The girl was still half-frostbitten, her consciousness fragmented into seventeen pieces, most of them scattered in the administrative vaults beneath the Lampwick Quarter. "I cannot restore you," Vrekka said, and it cost her more than gold ever had. "The pieces are too fractured, held in locks I cannot break."

The girl—her name was Massa, and she was maybe eight winters old—stared at the vials surrounding them. "Could you... could you ask them why they stay?"

Vrekka, a creature of pure accumulation, understood for the first time what a fae-touched druid had tried to teach her months before: some things cannot be held. Only witnessed.

stories.title: The Cartographer's Bright Lie
stories.text:
Henryk had burned out his own eyes to prevent the completion of the ninth map. But blindness didn't stop the prophecy—it only changed the shape of the lie he had to tell. The Dominion sent the Apprentice-Arcanist to the counter-archive's hidden library north of Pelimor, where Henryk sat with three young cartographers, tracing false geographies onto blank parchment using only touch and memory. "The prophecy-ledgers are growing unbearable," the Arcanist said. "They're predicting the tenth Ascension with certainty now. You must complete the ninth map so we can negotiate with whatever comes next. Show me the true cartography."

Henryk smiled with the face of a man who could no longer see his own reflection. "The ninth map cannot be completed," he said. "Not because I burned my eyes—that was theater, really—but because you're all asking the wrong question."

"Which is?"

"You assume prophecy is a landscape waiting to be discovered. But maps create the world they describe. Every cartographer who completes a map makes it real.

stories.title: The Glassblower's Last Defiance
stories.text: Thyra had burned her hands three times before the Remaking. After it, she burned them every day. In the Lampwick Quarter of Keshtir, beneath the furnace-houses where the Dominion forged consciousness-fragments into weapons-glass, she worked a different fire. While auditors tallied consciousness-vessels in the vaults above, Thyra sang the old furnace-songs—the ones her grandmother had carved into her memory before dying at a picket line. The fragments screamed when you melted them wrong. She'd learned to recognize the frequency: a high, crystalline wail like children calling through water. Most glass-forgers learned to ignore it. Thyra learned to listen. "You're slowing the output," Sella warned, appearing at the kiln-mouth with two steaming vessels. "They're counting pieces again. She was binding a consciousness-fragment—this one a merchant's third-self, scattered when the world fractured—into glass that would NOT hold a killing-edge. Instead, the fragment pulsed with something else. Recognition. Memory. A fragment that remembered it was whole. "Let them count," Thyra said.

stories.title: The Deepkin Diplomat's Mirror
stories.text:
Thalia had three faces now, and only one could speak. The Tear of the Drowned God was failing. Every reflection in the Sapphire Deep showed the same: the great seal, ancient beyond kingdoms, was cracking. In the deepest council chamber of the Sapphire Deep, where living coral platforms bloomed with bioluminescent gardens, three versions of Thalia sat around a table that had never been designed for contradiction. Thalia-First (the diplomat): "We renew the blood-covenant as our ancestors did. Five willing souls, taken at the turning of seasons. It has held for a thousand years."

Thalia-Second (the scholar): "It has cost us a thousand souls. There is another path—a daily covenant. Each day, we choose renewal instead of paying in death."

Thalia-Third (the warrior): "A choice cannot bind. Blood is binding. Blood is *real*."

The Keeper-of-Pearls watched from her throne of black coral. She was dying—they all were, slowly, as the abyss beneath the seal began to remember what it contained. Something old. Something that had been sealed, not killed.

stories.title: The Wyvern's Ledger
stories.text:
Sorrath had kept the same ledger for three centuries. Every coin entered, every treasured object catalogued in obsidian ink on pre-Remaking parchment. A king's hoard, documented with a merchant's precision. Gold turned to dust. Not gradually—instantly, as if reality had simply decided that value itself was negotiable. The mountain of coins became a dune of ash. The gems remained gems, but who wanted gems when consciousness-fragments were now the only currency that mattered? The tapestries, the crowns, the weapons forged by dead smiths—all of it, suddenly ornament. Suddenly memory. Sorrath sat in her cavern in the Ironspine Mountains, surrounded by three hundred years of accumulation, and she *laughed*. Then she wept. A refugee family found her like that, huddled in a shaft of light that cut through the ash-gold dust. They were starving. Their child had a fever. They saw the cavern and saw only shelter. Sorrath saw them and saw her own redundancy. "Take what you want," she told them. "It's all useless."

The eldest daughter stepped forward carefully.

stories.title: The Thief-Widow's Second Compass
stories.text:
Sorenna had sworn never to craft another compass after her husband died at the pre-human boundary. Cartography was for the living, she'd said. The dead need no direction. She offered pre-Remaking silk, three vials of starlight sealed in amber, and a name: "Kelvan. My brother. He's trapped in the Wailing Scar."

Sorenna didn't ask why a merchant's sister would hire a bone-carver to steal from the Dominion. She already knew. The Remaking had scattered everything—families, timelines, identities. Kelvan existed in three versions now, simultaneously alive in three worlds that were diverging like cracks in old glass. His sister wanted to pull him back to a single timeline before the Wailing Scar collapsed entirely. It required a compass. Not one that pointed north. One that pointed *home*—across the fractured boundaries, to the version of him that remembered loving her. Sorenna took the work. She carved the second compass from bone her dead husband had hidden before the Remaking—bone he'd meant to be her grave-good, if she died first.

stories.title: The Shepherd's Vigil
stories.text: Kestran had kept his flocks on the high meadows of the Steppe Marches for forty winters. The boundary-stones marked the edge of his domain—ancient markers carved with syllables in the Elder Tongue, placed there before kingdoms learned to speak. On one side, the wild grasslands where his sheep grazed. On the other, the wastes where the pre-human dead whispered in frequencies no living throat could match. Since the Remaking, the stones had been singing. Not in rage. In *question*. The boundaries were thinning. The dead were waking, and they weren't sure anymore what they were waking into. Kestran had never been a scholar or a bone-singer. He was a shepherd—the kind of man who understood animals the way most people understand fear, by living inside it daily. So when the boundary began to crack, he did what shepherds do: he kept vigil. Every night for three months, he brought his crook—carved from thorn-wood and bound with singing-bone by his grandmother's hands—and he stood between his flocks and the stones. He didn't sing to strengthen the boundary.
